opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the most important reason is very simple: our world was built for humans. Our homes, our offices, our hospitals, our streets: the stairs, the door handles, the kitchen counters, the light switches, the tools we use. Everything is designed around the size, the reach, and the movement of the human body. So if you want a robot to operate in that environment without rebuilding the environment, the humanoid form is a natural choice. It can open the same doors, climb the same stairs, and use the same tools we do.

The second reason is data and learning. In the age of embodied AI, a robot learns a lot by watching people, from videos, from demonstrations, from teleoperation. If the robot has a body structure similar to ours, with two arms, two hands, and a head with cameras roughly where our eyes are, it becomes much easier to transfer human behavior to the robot. The mapping is more direct. That's very valuable when you're trying to train a general-purpose model rather than program one task at a time.

Third, there's the social and emotional dimension. In a home, especially when you think about elderly care, which is a huge issue in China and many other aging societies, people are more comfortable interacting with something that has a familiar form. They can read its gestures, understand where it's looking, anticipate what it's going to do. That makes interaction more intuitive and, I think, safer.

That said, I don't believe humanoid is the only answer. For many specific tasks, a wheeled base, a robotic arm, or a vacuum robot is cheaper, more reliable, and more efficient. Autonomous vehicles are really robots too, and they don't look like people at all. So I see it as a spectrum. For specialized, single tasks, use specialized forms. But if you want one general-purpose machine that can do many things in a human environment, the humanoid form makes a lot of sense. The challenge now is cost, reliability, dexterity of the hands, and safety. Those still have a long way to go, but the progress in the last two or three years has been remarkable.

r002.rationale: It explains that homes, offices, and other environments are designed around the human body, so humanoid robots can use existing doors, stairs, and tools without rebuilding the environment.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest answer is that the world we live in was built by humans, for humans. Our doors, our stairs, our kitchens, the height of a table, the shape of a doorknob, the width of a hallway, all of it assumes a body roughly like ours. If you want a robot to work inside that environment without rebuilding the environment, the most practical thing is to give it a body that already fits. A humanoid can climb the stairs that are already there, open the drawer that is already there, use the tools that are already there. We don't have to redesign the home around the machine.

The second reason is data. Over the past few years we have learned that these systems improve dramatically when you can feed them large amounts of relevant experience. For a humanoid, the richest source of that experience is us. There are billions of hours of video of humans walking, cooking, carrying things, folding clothes, interacting with each other. If the robot's body is close to a human body, that data transfers much more directly. You can learn from demonstration, from motion capture, from teleoperation, and the mapping is natural. With a very different form factor you lose a lot of that.

The third reason is about generality. Special-purpose robots are wonderful at one task, and they will remain important in factories and logistics. But a home is not one task. It is thousands of small, unpredictable tasks in a cluttered space. A single general body that can handle most of them is more valuable than a dozen specialized devices. And the humanoid form is, as far as we know, the one body that has already proven it can do essentially everything a household requires.

And I would add a social dimension. People find it easier to interact with, to instruct, and to trust something whose movements and gestures they can read intuitively. When a humanoid turns its head, reaches out a hand, steps aside in a corridor, we understand what it intends without a manual. That matters a great deal if these machines are going to live alongside elderly people, children, families.

Now, I want to be honest that this is a bet, not a certainty. Humanoids are mechanically hard, they are expensive today, and bipedal balance is still a difficult problem. There are serious people who think wheels and simpler arms will win on cost for a long time. I think both will coexist. But if you ask me where the long-term center of gravity is for robots in human society, I believe it is the humanoid form, precisely because the society itself is human-shaped.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that our world is designed around the human body. In a home, the doors, stairs, furniture, and tools are all arranged for people. A robot with a similar shape can potentially use that environment without requiring us to redesign everything around it.

Two hands allow it to manipulate objects, and legs allow it to move through spaces that can be difficult for wheels. A familiar form may also make interaction more intuitive: people can understand where the robot is looking or what it is reaching for.

That doesn’t mean every robot should be humanoid. For a specific task, a simpler design may be better. But if you want a general-purpose robot that can help with many different activities in homes and society, the human form is a useful starting point.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that our world is designed around the human body. Doors, stairs, kitchens, tools—everything assumes a certain height, reach, and way of moving. If we want robots to work in those environments, the humanoid form is a useful choice because we don’t have to redesign the entire environment around them.

There’s also the interaction side. People can demonstrate a task with their hands or gestures, and a robot with a similar body has a natural way to reproduce it. That can make collaboration more intuitive.

But I wouldn’t say every robot needs to look like a human. For a specific task, a simpler design may be more efficient. The appeal of humanoids is their potential versatility: one robot that can move through our spaces and help with many different tasks. The real test is whether it can do those tasks safely, reliably, and at an affordable cost.
